pl-l4d15c7-d1e112.summary: Grants another reading: good works done by one who is evil and persists in mortal sin for a time or to the end are said to be rewarded and not forgotten, not for obtaining eternal life but for a more tolerable punishment at the judgment. Augustine says of a schismatic without charity who suffers for Christ out of fear of hell: his patience is praiseworthy, his judgment perhaps more tolerable; 'it profits me nothing' means nothing for the kingdom, not for a lighter punishment.
claims: Good works without charity lessen punishment but do not merit life.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e124.summary: Adds Augustine: this is said because of charity, without which true penance cannot be in us, since in the good the charity of God bears all things.
claims: True penance requires charity.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e130.summary: Concludes that goods done without charity profit for a more tolerable punishment but not for obtaining life.
claims: Works without charity mitigate punishment only.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e133.summary: Cites Ezekiel: if the just turns from justice and does iniquity, none of his just deeds will be remembered; he will die in his sin. So works done in charity are not in God's memory if one falls and does not rise.
claims: Merits are lost for one who dies unrepentant.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e137.summary: Quotes Gregory on this: when we commit evil, we vainly recall past goods, since in committing evil there should be no confidence in past goods.
claims: Past goods give no confidence in present sin.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e146.summary: Interprets: past goods give no confidence for receiving life, though they may for a milder punishment; otherwise it would contradict Augustine. Goods done without charity, accompanied by mortal guilt not removed by later penance, profit for a milder punishment, not the fruit of life.
claims: Past goods may mitigate punishment but do not secure life.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e149.summary: Considers that those who assert that penance and pardon are given for one crime while another is kept in delight or not confessed have been sufficiently answered.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e152.summary: Adds that they are refuted not only by the preceding authorities but by those that follow.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e155.summary: Quotes Augustine: many repent of having sinned but keep some sins in which they delight, not noticing that the Lord freed the mute and deaf together; he never healed by halves, casting out seven demons and a legion entirely, healing the whole man; the penitent must grieve for every crime. How could one who keeps a crime receive pardon for another? Without the love of God none finds grace; it is impiety to hope for half a pardon from him who is just. True penance tries to lead back to baptismal purity; let whoever repents repent of everything.
claims: One must repent of all sins.
Hoping for half a pardon is impious.
True penance aims at baptismal purity.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e164.summary: Adds Augustine: penitents, if you truly repent and do not mock, change your life; if you repent, why do you do again what you did wrongly? If you still do it, you are not a penitent.
claims: Continuing in sin shows penance is not real.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e171.summary: Quotes Innocent II: we warn our brothers not to let lay souls be deceived by false penances and drawn to hell; it is false penance when penance is done for one sin while others are disregarded, or for one without departing from another.
claims: Penance for one sin while retaining others is false.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e177.summary: Concludes that the preceding gives clear knowledge of true penance and satisfaction.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e180.summary: Defines: true penance is that which abolishes sin, which only penance that corrects the crime does; and that corrects the crime which brings hatred of the crime committed and of committing it, with desire to satisfy.
claims: True penance abolishes sin.
It brings hatred of sin and desire to satisfy.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e183.summary: Cites Judas, who is said to have repented without obtaining pardon, since such penance did not correct the crime.
claims: Judas's penance did not correct the crime.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e186.summary: Quotes Jerome: penance profited Judas nothing, since he could not correct his crime by it; if a brother so sins that he cannot amend it, he can be forgiven, but if the works remain, penance is assumed in word in vain; Judas could not amend his betrayal and added the crime of his own murder.
claims: Penance profits nothing if the crime is not corrected.

pl-l4d15c7-d1e195.summary: Explains that 'amend' here means not compensation for what was taken but reproach and abhorrence of the offense with desire to satisfy; one may unjustly take what cannot be restored, an eye or a life, and still be pardoned if he repents with love of worthy satisfaction. But one who unjustly took another's property and can restore it does not truly repent until he restores it; as long as it is not returned when it can be, penance is not done but feigned.
claims: Amendment means detesting sin with desire to satisfy.
Restorable goods must be restored for penance to be true.

pl-l4d15c7.summary: Grants that good works done while in mortal sin are 'remembered' by God not for eternal life but for a more tolerable punishment, as Augustine says of a schismatic who suffers for Christ without charity. Good works done in charity are forgotten if one falls and does not rise, as Ezekiel and Gregory say, though they may lessen punishment. This answers those who say pardon is given for one crime while another is retained or unconfessed. Augustine: Christ healed the whole man and cast out all demons, so one must repent of all sins; it is impiety to hope for half a pardon; Innocent II calls false the penance done for one sin while others are kept. True penance abolishes sin by hatred of the crime and desire to satisfy; Judas repented without pardon because his penance did not correct the crime. Correction means not restoring what cannot be restored but detesting the sin with desire to satisfy, though stolen goods that can be returned must be returned or penance is feigned.
claims: Good works without charity lessen punishment but do not merit life.
Good works done in charity are lost if one dies unrepentant.
One must repent of all sins; half a pardon is impossible.
True penance includes hatred of sin and desire to satisfy.
Stolen goods must be restored if possible, or penance is feigned.
